title: Start a Chicago Backyard Garden
description: From balcony pots to raised beds on a city lot — lead-safe soil, Zone 5/6 timing, and beginner crops that work in Chicago yards.

sub_paths.label: 🪣 Balcony & Patio Pots
sub_paths.description: Under 100 sq ft — pots, grow bags, fire escapes & porches

sub_paths.label: 🛏️ Small Raised Beds
sub_paths.description: 1–3 raised beds on a Chicago lot (lead-safe soil mix)

sub_paths.label: 🌿 Full Backyard Beds
sub_paths.description: 400–1,000 sq ft — mixed raised beds on a city lot

sub_paths.label: 🪴 Double Lot / Shared Yard
sub_paths.description: Bigger city lot or shared backyard — rotation & succession planting

bg_site.title: Choose Your Chicago Site
bg_site.summary: Sun, hose access, and lead-safe growing space decide whether a city garden thrives before you plant a single seed.
checklist: Walk your yard or patio at 9am, noon, and 3pm — note where full sun lands for 6+ hours
Prefer raised beds or containers over digging native Chicago soil until you know lead levels
Pick a spot within hose-reach of an outdoor spigot (or plan for watering cans upstairs)
Call 811 before you dig for any in-ground beds
Check condo / landlord rules if you are on a balcony, porch, or parkway
bg_site.ai_prompt_suggestion: How do I find the sunniest safe spot for a vegetable garden on a Chicago lot?

bg_soil.title: Lead-Safe Soil Basics
bg_soil.summary: Chicago lots often have contaminated soil — test first, then grow in clean raised-bed mix.
checklist: Get an urban soil lead test (extension lab or home kit) before growing food in native ground
If lead is a concern, use raised beds lined with landscape fabric and filled with bagged vegetable mix + compost
Do the jar test on any native soil: sand/silt/clay layers after overnight settling
Check drainage: dig a 12-inch hole, fill with water, time how long it drains
Mulch paths so kids and pets do not track bare city soil indoors
bg_soil.ai_prompt_suggestion: How do I test Chicago soil for lead and set up safe raised beds?

bg_containers.title: Set Up Your Container Garden
bg_containers.summary: The right container + the right mix is everything — most beginner failures come from soil that compacts or pots that don't drain.
checklist: Use containers at least 12 inches deep for tomatoes and peppers; 8 inches for herbs and greens
Drill or punch drainage holes if the pot doesn't have them — no drainage = root rot
Fill with a light potting mix (not garden soil — it compacts in pots)
Place in your sunniest spot; south- or west-facing walls reflect extra heat
Water when the top 1 inch of soil is dry — containers dry out 2–3× faster than beds
Feed with a balanced liquid fertilizer every 2 weeks (containers need more frequent feeding)
Top tomato picks for containers: Tumbling Tom, Sweet 100, Patio; greens: any lettuce, spinach, Swiss chard
bg_containers.ai_prompt_suggestion: What vegetables grow best in containers on a patio or balcony?

bg_beds_small.title: Build 1–3 Raised Beds
bg_beds_small.summary: A 4×8 raised bed is the most productive small-space garden unit — warm soil, no compaction, full weed control.
checklist: Start with one 4×8 ft bed — you can always add more once you know what you're doing
Cedar, Douglas fir, or composite lumber are best (avoid pressure-treated for veggies)
Build sides 10–12 inches tall for most crops; 18 inches for root crops
Fill with: 60% topsoil, 30% compost, 10% coarse perlite or aged wood chips
Level the ground before placing; put cardboard underneath to kill grass
Install a soaker hose or drip line before filling — much easier now than later
Mulch the top 2–3 inches with straw or shredded leaves after planting
bg_beds_small.ai_prompt_suggestion: What size raised beds should I build and what should I fill them with?

bg_beds_medium.title: Plan Your Bed Layout
bg_beds_medium.summary: At 400–1,000 sq ft you have room for a real kitchen garden — plan beds by family to make rotation easier.
checklist: Group beds by plant family: nightshades, brassicas, legumes, roots, cucurbits
Leave 18–24 inch paths between beds — wide enough to kneel and work
Put tallest plants (tomatoes, corn, beans on trellis) on the north side so they don't shade shorter crops
Build 3–5 raised beds or define rows with string and stakes
Install a simple drip or soaker system per zone — split by water-need (heavy vs light feeders)
Reserve one bed for perennial herbs (basil, oregano, chives, thyme) — plant once, harvest forever
Add compost 2–3 inches thick before every season
bg_beds_medium.ai_prompt_suggestion: How do I lay out a 600 sq ft kitchen garden for a family of four?

bg_beds_large.title: Plan Large-Scale Layout & Rotation
bg_beds_large.summary: Over 1,000 sq ft you're in small-plot territory — row spacing, rotation blocks, and water management matter.
checklist: Divide the space into 4 rotation blocks (nightshades / brassicas / legumes / roots+cucurbits)
Space rows 18–24 inches apart for most crops; 36 inches for sprawling squash and melons
Plan water access: a 1-acre garden needs 1,000+ gallons per week in summer
Install drip tape on a timer to reduce labor and fungal disease from overhead watering
Mark perennial zones (asparagus, berries, herbs) at the edge so they don't interfere with annual rotation
Build a simple compost area large enough to turn 500+ lbs of material at once
Consider a deer fence (8 ft or electric) before investing significant money in plants
bg_beds_large.ai_prompt_suggestion: How do I plan a large backyard garden with crop rotation?

bg_plant_beginner.title: Start with the Easy Wins
bg_plant_beginner.summary: Begin with crops that forgive mistakes — nail these first, then add challenging ones.
checklist: Easiest first crops: zucchini, bush beans, cherry tomatoes, lettuce, radishes, basil
Direct sow beans, radishes, and lettuce straight in the ground — no transplanting needed
Buy tomato and pepper transplants from a nursery your first year instead of starting from seed
Plant after your last frost date (ask your AI for the exact date for your location)
Thin seedlings to the spacing on the packet — crowded plants produce less
Label every row with a stake — you will forget what you planted where
bg_plant_beginner.ai_prompt_suggestion: What are the easiest vegetables for a first-time gardener to grow?

bg_plant_full.title: Full Planting Calendar
bg_plant_full.summary: Match every crop to the right season window — most failures are from planting too early or too late.
checklist: Find your last spring frost date — ask your AI assistant for your exact location
Cool-season crops (lettuce, spinach, peas, kale): plant 4–6 weeks before last frost
Warm-season crops (tomatoes, peppers, squash, beans): plant 1–2 weeks after last frost
Start tomatoes and peppers indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost
Fall planting: count 8–10 weeks back from your first fall frost date for greens and root crops
Keep a paper or digital journal with what you planted, when, and the result
bg_plant_full.ai_prompt_suggestion: What should I plant now based on my frost dates?

bg_water.title: Watering & Mulching
bg_water.summary: Consistent moisture (not soggy, not bone dry) is the single biggest yield driver after sunlight.
checklist: Water at the base of plants — wet leaves overnight cause fungal disease
Deep and less often beats shallow and daily: 1 inch per week total is the target
Check soil moisture with your finger — 2 inches down should feel like a wrung-out sponge
Install a timer on your soaker hose or drip line and forget it (set for early morning)
Mulch with 2–3 inches of straw, shredded leaves, or wood chips to cut watering by 50%
Newly transplanted seedlings need water every day for 1–2 weeks until roots establish
Signs of overwatering: yellow leaves, mushy stems. Signs of underwatering: wilting in morning.
bg_water.ai_prompt_suggestion: How often should I water my vegetable garden and what is the best method?

bg_pests_easy.title: Simple Pest Prevention
bg_pests_easy.summary: For small gardens the best defense is observation — catch problems early and most never become catastrophic.
checklist: Walk the garden every 2–3 days and look at leaf undersides (aphids, caterpillar eggs live there)
Pinch off any chewed or spotted leaves before problems spread
Float row covers over young transplants for the first 2–3 weeks (keeps most flying pests off)
Hand-pick tomato hornworms — they're large and easy to remove
Spray with diluted dish soap + water for aphid outbreaks (1 tsp soap per quart water)
Interplant marigolds — they deter many common pests and attract beneficials
bg_pests_easy.ai_prompt_suggestion: How do I keep pests off my small vegetable garden without chemicals?

bg_pests.title: Organic Pest & Disease Management
bg_pests.summary: A proactive IPM system beats reactive spraying — build habitat for beneficials and scout weekly.
checklist: Install a 'beneficial insect hotel' or let a patch of dill and fennel go to flower — lacewings and parasitic wasps will follow
Scout every week: check leaf undersides, stems, and soil around the base
Use floating row covers on brassicas from transplant until bolting
Neem oil (1 tbsp per gallon water + a few drops soap) handles most soft-bodied pests and early fungal issues
Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) spray targets caterpillars without harming bees or earthworms
Copper fungicide for early/late blight on tomatoes — preventive spray every 7–10 days in wet weather
Rotate crops so the same family never occupies the same bed two years in a row
bg_pests.ai_prompt_suggestion: What organic sprays and methods control common vegetable garden pests?

bg_harvest.title: Harvest & What to Do With It
bg_harvest.summary: Harvest at the right time and your plants produce more — most beginners leave vegetables on the plant too long.
checklist: Harvest zucchini at 6–8 inches — oversized zucchini signals the plant to stop producing
Pick tomatoes when fully colored and slightly soft — don't let them split on the vine
Snip basil and herbs weekly to prevent flowering (once it flowers, flavor declines)
Harvest beans when pods snap cleanly — don't let them dry on the plant mid-season
Store most vegetables in the fridge immediately after harvest to preserve quality
Eat or preserve surplus within 2–3 days for peak nutrition
bg_harvest.ai_prompt_suggestion: How do I know when my vegetables are ready to harvest?

bg_seeds.title: Seed Saving Basics
bg_seeds.summary: Save open-pollinated seed from your best plants and your garden improves year over year.
checklist: Only save seed from open-pollinated or heirloom varieties — hybrid seeds won't reproduce true
Let one tomato, pepper, or bean plant fully mature past eating stage to collect seed
Ferment tomato seeds in water 2–3 days, rinse, dry on paper plates
Store dry seeds in labeled paper envelopes inside an airtight container in a cool dark place
Most vegetable seeds stay viable 3–5 years if stored below 50°F
bg_seeds.ai_prompt_suggestion: How do I save vegetable seeds for next year?

bg_rotation.title: Crop Rotation & Cover Crops
bg_rotation.summary: Move plant families each season to break disease cycles and build long-term soil fertility.
checklist: Map your garden into 4 zones and rotate: nightshades → brassicas → legumes → roots+cucurbits → back
Never plant tomatoes or peppers in the same soil two years in a row (prevents blight and nematode buildup)
Plant a winter cover crop after fall harvest: winter rye or crimson clover
Mow cover crops and let them decompose 2–3 weeks before spring planting
Keep records of what grew where — a simple notebook or phone photo of each bed label is enough
bg_rotation.ai_prompt_suggestion: How do I set up a crop rotation plan for my backyard garden?

title: Join a Chicago Community Garden
description: Get a shared plot, learn the rules, grow with neighbors, and keep a small city bed productive all season.
target_audience: Chicago neighbors joining or tending a community garden plot

cg_find.title: Find & Join a Garden
cg_find.summary: Chicago has neighborhood and park-district gardens with waitlists, orientation, and plot fees.
checklist: Search Chicago Park District and neighborhood gardens near your zip code
Ask about plot size, annual fee, water access, and tool sharing
Attend orientation — most gardens require it before you dig
Get on the waitlist early (many open applications in late winter)
cg_find.ai_prompt_suggestion: How do I join a community garden plot in Chicago?

cg_rules.title: Plot Rules & Neighbors
cg_rules.summary: Shared gardens succeed when everyone follows watering, weeding, and end-of-season cleanup rules.
checklist: Read the garden handbook: organic-only? fence height? tall crops allowed?
Learn watering schedule and whether hoses are shared or timed
Keep paths clear and weeds pulled so neighbors are not fighting seeds
Mark your plot and respect boundary lines
cg_rules.ai_prompt_suggestion: What are typical Chicago community garden rules for new plot holders?

cg_soil.title: Safe Soil in Shared Beds
cg_soil.summary: Even community plots can sit on urban fill — know what you are planting into.
checklist: Ask garden leadership whether beds use clean fill / raised soil or native ground
Add compost only if the garden allows outside materials
Mulch bare soil to reduce splash and tracking
Wash produce well; peel root crops grown in older soil if lead risk is unknown
cg_soil.ai_prompt_suggestion: How do Chicago community gardens handle soil safety and compost?

cg_plant.title: Plant a Small Shared Plot
cg_plant.summary: Prioritize high-yield crops that fit a 10×10 or similar plot without shading neighbors.
checklist: Sketch a simple layout: tall crops on the north side of the plot
Start with tomatoes, peppers, greens, beans, and herbs
Use trellises for cucumbers/beans to save floor space
Leave room to walk so you do not compact wet soil
cg_plant.ai_prompt_suggestion: What crops fit a small Chicago community garden plot?

cg_season.title: Season Care & Cleanup
cg_season.summary: Weekly visits keep weeds down; fall cleanup keeps your plot for next year.
checklist: Visit at least weekly in summer — water, harvest, and pull weeds
Share surplus with neighbors or a local food pantry when allowed
Clear spent plants by the garden's fall deadline
Ask about winter plot holding fees and spring signup dates
cg_season.ai_prompt_suggestion: How do I keep a Chicago community garden plot productive through the season?

title: Sell at Chicago Farmers Markets
description: Bring backyard or garden surplus to neighborhood markets — products, Illinois cottage food rules, SNAP/Link Match, and listing on Chicago Ag Connect.
target_audience: Chicago growers ready to sell at neighborhood markets
cta_label: List Your Booth on Chicago Ag Connect

sm_products.title: Choose What to Sell
sm_products.summary: Focus on 3–5 products that fit a small city growing space and sell well at Chicago markets.
checklist: List your top crops by yield from a backyard or community plot
Visit 2–3 Chicago markets on Saturday and note what sells out
Calculate cost per unit including seeds, packaging, transit, and booth fee
Consider herbs, greens, tomatoes, and simple value-added items if cottage-food eligible
sm_products.ai_prompt_suggestion: What products sell best at Chicago farmers markets for a small backyard grower?

sm_labeling.title: Labeling & Food Safety
sm_labeling.summary: Meet Illinois cottage food and market labeling requirements before your first booth day.
checklist: Check Illinois cottage food rules for products allowed without a commercial kitchen
Create labels with product name, ingredients, net weight, and your grower name
Ask your market manager about food-handler certificates and insurance
Keep simple batch records for anything you process
sm_labeling.ai_prompt_suggestion: What Illinois cottage food labeling rules apply at Chicago farmers markets?

sm_apply.title: Apply to Chicago Markets
sm_apply.summary: Many Chicago markets fill vendor spots months before the season opens.
checklist: Contact market managers in fall/winter for the following summer season
Prepare photos of your produce, setup, and growing space
Ask about SNAP/Link Match and whether you need to enroll as a vendor
Plan harvest and transit so produce stays cool on CTA / car / bike market days
sm_apply.ai_prompt_suggestion: How do I apply to sell at Chicago farmers markets?

sm_list.title: List on Chicago Ag Connect
sm_list.summary: Help neighbors find your booth by posting market days and products each week.
checklist: Create a vendor profile on Chicago Ag Connect
Report which Chicago market you will attend each week
List products so shoppers can search for what you sell
Mention if you accept SNAP / Link Match
sm_list.ai_prompt_suggestion: How do I set up my vendor profile on Chicago Ag Connect?
